nothing worth writing"* after finding a comparison that would in fact kill the
mutant.

So the rule, now in every brief:

> **A sentence containing "only", "exactly one", "nothing else", "never" or
> "cannot" is a measurement, not a description.** Either run the grep and cite
> it, or write the weaker sentence that does not need one.

**The rule worked prospectively within one commit of being written, which is
the first time any rule here has.** F-29's second rework reports that it *nearly
wrote a new false sentence* and caught itself: it was about to say
`HOST_CHARACTERS`' anchor **cannot** be falsified, then checked, and found that
it **can** — three near-miss patterns all anchor with `$`, so the trailing-newline
class separates them as shipped and stops doing so under the mutation. A test
comparing them *would* kill `$`.

What it wrote instead is the distinction that matters, and it is sharper than
the rule I gave it: such a test **would not be a pin**, because it asserts a
relationship nobody maintains between surfaces with no reason to agree. So the
docblock now says *pinned by nothing worth writing* rather than *unreachable by
any test* — a narrower claim, and a true one. It softened the block's opening
"cannot be falsified" to match, on the reasoning that that is *"the sentence a
reader counts from."*

Two smaller self-corrections in the same breath: the near-misses are **three**,
not the two it had been told — it found a third — and the line it cites is in
`RegistrableDomain::parse`, not `fromString`.

This is worth recording because every other instance of the quantifier rule in
this ledger is **retrospective** — a verifier finding a false "only" after the
fact. Here the author applied it to their own unwritten sentence and produced a
better claim than the one they were reaching for. The rule's value is not that
it catches false absolutes in review; it is that it makes the writer ask *"can
I cite this?"* before the sentence exists.

Two things make this more than a style note.

**These sentences are load-bearing in a way ordinary prose is not.** A wrong
description misleads one reader. A wrong *"only"* is what the next round's
scope is derived from — F-13's gap survived three verification rounds because
everyone read the disclosure and routed around an obstacle that did not exist.

**The good version already exists in the same reports.** F-13's own sole-caller
chain is the model: four links, each independently checkable by grep, three
true and one false — and because it was written as a chain of citable claims
rather than a summary, the false link was found in minutes instead of surviving
another round. The habit to keep is not "avoid strong claims", it is **make
strong claims falsifiable and cite the thing that falsifies them.**

### A pattern worth naming: the bound accepted on a reason that is not true

Two findings produced the same shape on the same day, by different agents on
different modules, and it is worth naming before it produces a third.

* **F-28.** A docblock said `verify_peer_name` *cannot* be pinned from that
  surface, naming the OS trust store as an obstacle a test cannot add to. Its
  verifier pinned it from exactly that surface — and the reason it could was the
  reason the docblock gave for why it could not.
* **F-13.** A commit left a real gap open — a token short of `Datastore.Audit`
  declared ready — on the ground that closing it would violate an architecture
  test. I told the rework to test that premise rather than accept it. The test
  refuses a capability **no product requirement names**; naming one satisfies it.
  The obstacle did not exist.

Both are **honestly disclosed bounds**, which is why neither was a rejection and
why both agents were doing what this programme asks. That is exactly what makes
the pattern dangerous. The programme's standing instruction is to name your
bounds rather than hide them, and a named bound is treated — correctly — as good
practice. But **a named bound carries an implicit claim that somebody checked**,
and in both of these nobody had. The disclosure then does the opposite of its
job: it converts an unexamined assumption into a documented decision, and the
next reader inherits it as settled.

So the instruction gains a clause, and it is now in every rework brief:

> **Name your bounds — and when you name one as an impossibility or as an
> obstacle imposed by something else, say what you tried.** A bound whose
> reason has not been tested is a guess wearing a disclosure's clothes.

**The operational form, which F-13's implementer wrote better than I did:**

> Treat any recorded reason of the shape ***"X would violate Y"* as unverified
> until Y has been opened** — and say in the report that you opened it.

That is sharper than my version because it is checkable. "Say what you tried" can
be satisfied with a sentence; "say that you opened Y" names the artifact and
either you did or you did not. In F-13's case the entire bound turned on the
difference between *"refuses a new capability"* and *"refuses an unconsumed
capability"*, which was one file away and had survived three verification rounds
unread. It is now in every rework and verification brief.

The cost of not doing this is asymmetric in a way worth spelling out. An
untested bound that turns out real costs one agent an hour of confirming it. An
untested bound that turns out false costs every subsequent round, because each
one reads the disclosure and routes around the thing that was never actually
shut. F-13's gap survived three verification rounds that way.

### Declining a database constraint that I required on F-04 — and why the two differ

F-33's implementer asked me directly whether to add a PostgreSQL exclusion
constraint as belt and braces, having established it would actually build
(`btree_gist` available, the role superuser) rather than calling it impossible.
It declined and offered to build it on my word.

**Ruling: do not build it.** Its reason (b) is the decisive one and it is right:
the constraint can express **only the in-pool realm**, because the realm
discriminator — `datacenter_id` and `scope` — lives on `ip_pools` and not on
`subnets`. So it would be a **second, partial answer** to "may this block
exist", refusing with a constraint violation where the action answers 422. That
is the precise anti-pattern `RegisterSubnetRequest`'s own docblock names, and
the one this round **just removed**: a weaker duplicate of a rule, disagreeing
with the real one at the edges and surfacing as a 500.

**This looks inconsistent with F-04, where I required exactly such a constraint,
and the distinction is worth stating because it will come up again.**

| | F-04's CHECK | F-33's proposed EXCLUDE |
|---|---|---|
| what it asserts | a **property of the column** — that the stored value is canonical | a **rule about the estate** — which blocks may coexist |
| completeness | **total**: every row, every path, no exceptions | **partial**: one of three realms, the other two inexpressible |
| relation to the action | the action's fold is *how* the property is achieved; the constraint is the property | the action's guard **is** the rule; the constraint is a second, weaker copy of part of it |
| when it fires | only if something bypasses the fold — i.e. a genuine invariant breach | on ordinary estates the action already refuses; it fires only where the two disagree |

So the test is not *"is a database constraint good?"* but **"is the constraint
the same rule, stated completely, or a different and narrower rule wearing the
same name?"** F-04's is the invariant the index depends on. F-33's would be a
subset that answers differently at the boundary — and a subset that disagrees
at the boundary is how this programme's worst defects have been built.

**What I accept as the residual**, named by the implementer rather than
discovered: the guard is at the action, and `LoadReferenceTopologyForSimulation`
(which refuses to run on production) and `SubnetFactory` bypass it, as would a
direct SQL insert. For a finding whose harm is *one address reaching two
customers through the operator route*, the route is the reachable path and a
hand-written INSERT is not a supported flow. Recorded, not required.

The **pre-existing** overlaps an estate may already hold are a different matter
and are genuinely not covered. The implementer identified `infra:preflight` as
the natural home for a report-don't-refuse check and deliberately did not touch
it while F-35 is in bounded rework on that exact surface — which is the right
call on cross-branch grounds, and is now on the integration list.

## Findings closed by another finding's branch

### F-47 — a candidate, checked far enough to be worth writing down and no further

F-47 is *"`DedicatedServerStatus::Retired` — three readers, one of them a race
argument, against zero production writers; only writer is a test factory."*

`remediation/f12` adds one. Its retire action does
`$locked->forceFill(['status' => DedicatedServerStatus::Retired])->save()` after
`assertCanTransition`, behind the row lock, with an audit row
(`AuditAction::DedicatedServerRetired`) — and F-12's round five then pinned the
state machine's *absence* of outward edges from `retired` with a test that drives
both orders through the endpoints.

So the finding's central claim stops being true the moment F-12 merges. **That is
not the same as F-47 being closed**, and I am recording it as a candidate rather
than a closure for two reasons: F-12 is itself still in verification, and F-47
names *three* readers including a race argument that nobody has re-read against
the new writer. Whoever takes F-47 starts by checking those three readers against
F-12's writer rather than by looking for a writer — the search is already done.

The general shape is worth naming: **a finding about something that does not
exist is closed by the branch that makes it exist, and that branch will not
mention it.** Before starting any remaining CODE_GAP finding, grep the open
branches for the symbol first.

### F-43 — read far enough to sharpen its brief, not to start it

`ConsoleSessionStore::consume()` (`src/Modules/Vps/Application/Services/`) really
does never compare `expires_at` with now: it reads the record, checks the token
hash, wins or loses an `add()` race on a consumed-marker, and returns a
`ConsoleSession` carrying the stored `expires_at` verbatim. Expiry is enforced
**only** by the TTL passed to `put()` and `add()`, so the guarantee is the cache
driver's and not the code's — which is exactly why the finding says the expiry
tests prove `ArrayStore` rather than the store in production. Its round should
begin by deciding whether the driver's TTL is an acceptable enforcement point
(and if so, pinning that claim against the driver the platform actually runs)
rather than by adding a comparison nobody asked for.


A repair aimed at one finding sometimes closes another outright. Recorded here
so the second is neither dispatched for duplicate work nor left reading `OPEN`
against code that already closes it. A finding in this table still needs its
own independent verification against its own text.

| Finding | Closed by | Evidence | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| **F-47** — `DedicatedServerStatus::Retired` is a legal transition target from three states, with an `isRetired()` predicate, an exclusion in the inventory sweep, and a concurrency comment in `SyncDedicatedServer.php:56` reasoning about a race against a state no production code can produce. Its only writer was a test factory: three readers against zero production writers. | `remediation/f12` | F-12's new `RetireDedicatedServer` (`POST /api/admin/dedicated/{server}/retire`, `dedicated.manage`, evidence required, audited) is that production writer. F-12's verifier drove it independently: a machine decommissioned, marked failed in the rack, then retired returns 200, the quarantine clock starts and the address comes back. | `CLOSED pending its own verification` — the writer exists and is reachable from a real operator act; what still needs checking at F-47's turn is whether the three *readers* are now truthful, in particular whether `SyncDedicatedServer`'s concurrency comment is still reasoning about an impossible state. **Neither the commit message nor the code names F-47**, which is how this nearly went unnoticed. |

## A fifth line for the sweep discipline: `numstat` is blind to a file that is new

Two rounds hit this independently in the same wave, which is what makes it a line
rather than an anecdote.

The discipline says *confirm `git diff HEAD --numstat` is non-empty before the run
counts* — the guard against a mutation that never landed. **For an untracked file
that check is worthless by definition**: `git diff HEAD` does not show a file git
has never seen, so the numstat is empty no matter what you wrote, or — worse —
**non-empty because of some other file entirely**, which is the shape F-37's round
hit. Its first sweep leaned on numstat alone with three of four mutated files new,
and the number it read was about the fourth.

F-11's round ten hit the same thing and said so at the time: for a new file the
authority is `git status --porcelain` showing `??`.

**The fifth line, adopted:** *prove a mutation landed by CONTENT HASH — pristine
sha ≠ mutated sha — and use `numstat` only as a secondary check on files git
already tracks.* For an untracked file, `git status --porcelain` is the landing
proof and the hash is still the restore proof.

This is the same family as the other four and the family now has a name: **every
one of them is a measurement instrument that reports success for a reason
unrelated to the thing being measured.** A green mutation line because the
mutation never landed. A guard that turned a run into a non-run. A proof step
that aborted under `pipefail` because `diff` exits 1 when files differ. And now a
diff that is blind to the file you just created.

## When a guard reimplements a framework's resolution, the enumeration is not closable

F-08 has now had five rounds, each closing exactly the axes named to it, and
each followed by a new one. Its seventh round said so itself — *"this is the
fourth time the hole moved one axis over… nobody has shown there is no fifth"* —
and I asked its verifier to go looking. **It found two more in an afternoon, with
no exotic knowledge**, and then answered the question I actually needed answered.

### The two, because they show the shape

- **A fail-open branch in a three-branch reading.** `isAWait()` ends
  `is_numeric($declared) ? (float) $declared > 0 : true`, so anything it cannot
  parse is taken as a wait. But `'0,0,0'` is Laravel's own wire format for a
  backoff ladder (`Queue::getJobBackoff()` implodes on commas,
  `Worker::calculateBackoff()` explodes on them), and a zeroed one is no ladder.
  `[0,0,0]` **is** caught; `'0,0,0'` is not.
- **A property that is not a property of the class at all.** `queueOf()` scans
  the class's own file for `onQueue(…)`; `Job::dispatch()->onQueue('payments')`
  puts it at the call site. No amount of reading the class can find it.

### The argument, which is the part worth keeping

> The guard reimplements, in a test, a resolution the framework performs at
> payload-construction time from four independent inputs — class declarations in
> three or four spellings each, attributes, trait and parent composition, and
> call-site builder methods — plus worker options. **The reimplementation has to
> be right about all of them; the framework only has to be right once.**

That is not a statement about F-08's diligence. Round seven's work was good: its
reproduction was a runtime measurement with a real worker, its mutants were
honest, and three of the eight caveats it handed its reviewer turned out to be
*over*-stated in its own favour. The mechanism was wrong, not the effort.

### The rule I am adopting from it

**When a gate's job is to predict what a framework will resolve at runtime, a
source reading is the wrong instrument, and widening it is not progress.** Each
widening passes its band, ships, and is followed by the next axis — five times
here, and the sixth was already visible.

The test for whether this rule applies: *can the value the gate is asserting
about be changed by something outside the file the gate reads?* For F-08 the
answer is yes in at least three ways (a call-site builder method, an attribute
on a parent, a supervisor's configuration). When the answer is yes, **read the
resolved value from where the framework has finished resolving it** — for F-08
that is `Queue::createPayloadUsing()`, which carries the already-resolved
`queue`, `maxTries`, `backoff` and `retryUntil`, the numbers the worker will
actually use. It closes both new axes *and* both of the round's own
runtime-invisible cases in one move.

**The bar was never the problem.** *"A deployment can no longer silently
reinstate F-08"* is the standard that exposed all of this, and it stays. Round
eight is dispatched to build the runtime reading — **explicitly not a sixth
widening** — and I will reject a sixth widening that arrives with a green band.

### Where else this applies, flagged now rather than after the fact

This programme has other gates that read source to predict runtime, and they
should be looked at against the test above before the re-audit, not after:
F-23's producer classifier (tokenises `src/` to decide which enum cases can be
written), F-15's payload census (scans `src/` for write shapes — and **has
already failed the same way twice**, on a heredoc and on a second writer in an
already-listed file), and F-29's anchor walk (tokenises a policy to enumerate
its regex anchors — and has already been falsified by a `\z` split across two
literals). The pattern is the same in all four: **a reading of the text
standing in for a property of the execution.** That does not make them wrong —
some properties have no runtime moment to read — but each should state which
kind it is.

## A fourth line for the sweep discipline, found by a verifier's own harness failing

F-12's verifier reported an instrument defect in its own tooling rather than
working around it, and it is a genuinely new member of the family this ledger
already carries at "a green mutation line can also mean the mutation never
landed" and "the guard protecting a measurement turned the run into a non-run".

Its harness printed the proof that a mutation had landed with

```sh
diff -u "$PRISTINE" "$TARGET" | sed -n '3,40p'
```

under `set -euo pipefail`. **`diff` exits 1 when the files differ — which is the
success case.** So `pipefail` killed the script at the line whose only job was to
prove the mutation had landed: after mutating, before running the band, before
restoring. It left a live mutant in the worktree and never ran anything, and it
presented as a *truncated log* rather than as an error.

The new member is sharper than its two predecessors. There the guard failed. Here
**the proof step itself was the thing that aborted the run**, and the abort
happened at the exact moment the tree was dirty.

It was caught only because the verifier checked the target's content hash after
the harness exited non-zero, found it differed from pristine, and restored by
copy plus hash. That is the discipline this ledger already requires — restore
from a pristine copy, verify by content hash, never by `git checkout` — working
exactly as intended, one layer down from where it was written for.

**The fourth line, adopted:** *any command whose non-zero exit is the success
signal must be wrapped `|| true` inside a `pipefail` harness.* `diff`, `grep`
with no match, `git diff --quiet`, `cmp` — all of them report "different" or
"absent" with a non-zero status, and all of them get used as proof steps.

## The row is ordered against the way it is read, and that has now cost a verification

Two agents in one wave caught me writing a brief from a ledger row that was not
about the round I was dispatching. After the second I stopped treating it as two
slips and measured it.

**Eight rows of forty-seven** advertise, in their status cell, a round their own
narrative never records: F-04, F-12, F-15, F-18, F-21, F-29, F-31, F-33. I did
not find that by reading. I found it by writing three lines that compare the
worktree slugs and shas quoted in each status cell against the text of the same
row's narrative — and the eight fell out immediately.

### The mechanism

A row's **narrative is appended** each round. Its **status cell is replaced**.
So the oldest narrative sits at the top, the newest round is represented by a
status cell alone, and a reader who skims the row gets the wrong round by
default. The row is ordered against the way it is read. Nothing about this is
exotic; it is the same shape as every unmeasured absolute in this document, and
I built it into the format myself.

### What it actually cost, which is more than embarrassment

- **F-15**: I told its verifier round four was *"fourteen commits answering a
  rejection on two grounds"*. Round four is **one commit**; the fourteen-commit
  stretch ends at `5517f80`, an ancestor of round three's tip. The verifier
  caught it, verified against what the row *does* record verbatim, and said in
  *could not establish* that it never saw round four's rejection text.
- **F-11**: I told its implementer *"the row states the five blocking items"*.
  It does not. `f11e`, `v11t`, *round nine* and *five blocking* appear in that
  row **zero times** — measured, not skimmed. The implementer looked for the
  record everywhere before concluding (every `.md` in the repository, the briefs
  directory, `git log --all`), then read the surviving scratch artefacts of the
  verifier that was supposed to have produced it, and found **agreement, not
  five blocks**: a clean baseline, the documented mutation reproducing exactly,
  and a planted second writer correctly caught.

**That verification is lost.** Not contradicted — lost. I cannot say whether
round eight was blocked on five items, on one, or on none, and the status cell
asserting five is withdrawn rather than restated. The empirical route is the
only one left: `v11u` verifies `ac7bbe2`, which sits on top of round eight, so a
verdict there covers both rounds' state. Archaeology would be guessing.

### The gate

`infrastructure/scripts/validate-ledger-rows.py`. Every slug and sha quoted in a
row's status cell must appear in that row's narrative. **It is red on today's
tree, on all eight rows, and I ran it red before writing a word of the fix** —
which is F-38's whole subject, applied to myself rather than to a CI step.

It is a deliberately weak check and the file says so: it cannot tell whether a
narrative is *accurate*, only whether the round its status advertises was ever
written down. F-15's defect — a narrative that exists and describes the wrong
round — would pass it. A weak check that runs beats a strong one that does not,
and the strong version is a person reading the row, which is the thing that
already failed twice.

### What I did about the agents already in flight

Five verifications were running against affected rows when I measured this
(F-04, F-12, F-21, F-29, F-33). I sent each one a correction naming its own
row's missing tokens, restating that the commit under verification has not
changed, and telling it to treat the narrative as history of earlier rounds
unless a paragraph names its sha. I did not ask any of them to reconstruct the
missing narrative — that is mine — and I told them to record it in
*could not establish* if the gap hampered them.

The thing I want to be honest about: **both instances were caught by the agent,
not by me.** The protocol held because two subordinate readers refused to accept
a brief that did not match the tree. That is one layer of luck too many to rely
on, which is why the gate exists now rather than a resolution to be careful.

## A brief of mine described the wrong round, and its verifier caught it

F-15's verifier opened its report by correcting me, and it was right.

I wrote in its dispatch that round four is *"fourteen commits answering a
rejection on two points"*, and told it to read those two grounds as its
requirements. Round four is **one commit**. `dd599c2` sits directly on
`5adfe1f`, round three's tip; the fourteen-commit stretch ends at `5517f80`,
which `git merge-base --is-ancestor 5517f80 5adfe1f` confirms is an **ancestor**
of round three's tip. I verified this myself rather than taking the correction
on trust, and the verifier's reading is exact.

Where it came from: the F-15 row's leading paragraph describes that earlier
round — its figures are 3,947 / 144,453, and the row itself records `5517f80`
at 3,947 against round three's tip at 3,956. **The row has no round-four
narrative at all**, only a status cell. I wrote the brief from the paragraph at
the top of the row and did not check that the paragraph was about the round I
was dispatching.

The mechanism is worth naming because it is not the same as the other
bookkeeping defects in this ledger. Those were claims that decayed. This one
was never true: a row that accumulates rounds top-down ends up with its **oldest**
narrative first and its newest round represented by a status cell, so the
reader who skims the row gets the wrong round by default. The row is ordered
against the way it is read.

Two consequences:

1. Every brief I write from a ledger row must name the **commit** the round is,
   and I must check that sha's parent against the round history before writing
   a word about what the round contains. F-15's dispatch for round five does
   this, and carries the correction explicitly so the next agent does not
   inherit my error the way this one nearly did.
2. This does not invalidate the verification. The verifier said so itself and
   then did the right thing: it verified round four against its own four stated
   corrections and against round three's carried-forward blocking item, which
   is what the ledger *does* record verbatim, and it flagged in
   *could not establish* that it never saw round four's actual rejection text
   because the ledger does not contain it. That is the correct response to a
   brief that is wrong — not to guess what I meant.

## The seventh stoppage: a container restart with thirteen agents in flight

The container was restarted with the whole pool working. The filesystem survived
entirely — the repository at `e9607c6`, all thirteen worktrees, the scratchpad —
and by now the procedure for this is routine. What it produced this time is
worth recording because the salvage found more than the last two did.

### What survived, measured rather than assumed

| | |
|---|---|
| Committed and safe | **F-42 round one** had already landed `b683fb5` — the only round that got a commit out before the restart |
| Uncommitted work worth keeping | six trees: `f04k`, `f14e`, `f29f`, `f33e`, `f36a`, `f37a` |
| Nothing started | `f11f`, and the four verifiers `v08h`, `v15i`, `v23a`, `v30a` |

### One live mutant, and it was in the one tree that had committed

`f42a` held `apps/web/src/test-setup.ts` at **0 added, 46 deleted** — a deletion
of the accessible-name warm-up block that its own commit `b683fb5` had just
added. That is **step four caught mid-measurement**: the round mutating its own
fix to show the flake returns, killed before it could restore. Restored, and
verified by reading the block back rather than by the command's exit status.

This is now the third stoppage in a row to leave a live mutant in a tree, and
the pattern is stable enough to state as a rule: **the tree most likely to hold
a live mutant is the tree that has made the most progress**, because step four
comes after the fix and a round that has not reached step three has nothing to
mutate. Survey the furthest-along trees first, not the untouched ones.

### And a near-miss of my own, in the opposite direction

`f29f` held a five-line edit to `EndpointPolicy.php`, and `f29f` is the round I
had explicitly briefed to *plant a split anchor and see the partition row green*.
Everything about the shape said live mutant. I read it before touching it, and
it is the **fix**: the numeral "seven" removed from a sentence and replaced with
a statement that the list is the only place holding the count. Had I restored it
on the strength of the tree's identity and the diff's size, I would have
destroyed the round's actual work while congratulating myself on the discipline.

**Reading the diff is the discipline. Recognising the tree is not.**

### The salvage commits, and why they are labelled the way they are

Each of the six is committed to its own branch as a
`WIP SALVAGE — an interrupted round, NOT a delivered round` commit whose message
states plainly that no test was run against that state, no first-fail proof is
claimed, no mutation was performed or restored, and the eight-step protocol is
incomplete. The risk this guards against is specific: a half-finished round
sitting on a branch looks exactly like a finished one to the next reader, and
this ledger's own status cells have already proved that a claim outlives the
thing it describes. The label is in the commit message because that is the one
place a future reader cannot fail to see it.

Full diffs and untracked files also went to `scratchpad/crash-salvage-6/` before
anything was committed, belt and braces, because the commit itself could have
been the thing that was interrupted.

### What the salvage tells me about the rounds themselves

Two are worth naming, because they show the work was on the right track and the
re-dispatch should build on it rather than restart it:

- **`f14e` (F-14 round fourteen) had already written the remedy its verifier
  named.** The rule is renamed `namesAYearBeyondTheOneItsDateAlreadyNames()` —
  the verifier's own words — the clock regex is corrected so the fractional tail
  binds to the seconds group (Family C), a five-or-more-digit run is tested
  (Family B's glued join), and a semantic check compares the parsed year with
  and without the last numeric field. That is the shape, not a fourth patch.
- **`f04k` (F-04 round seven) had built the missing clause**: a
  `ResetHostingAccountPassword` action, its refusal exception, a feature test,
  and a `PanelThatLosesItsAnswer` double — which is exactly the lost-answer case
  the blocking item is about.

## The relaunch, and two live edits waiting in the trees to be committed by somebody else

Eleven agents dispatched after the sixth stoppage, on the user's explicit
instruction. The thirteen-slot pool is saturated and isolation holds: each agent
has its own worktree, its own `remediation/*` branch, its own
`lynomia_test_<slug>` database and its own Redis index, all thirteen distinct
(checked against `/home/user/worktrees/.redis-slots`, not assumed).

| Slot | Role | Subject |
|---|---|---|
| `v04j` `v12j` `v14l` `v15g` `v20b` `v21c` `v29k` | verification | F-04 r6 `544b142`, F-12 r7 `61409f1`, F-14 r13 `f6bea44`, F-15 r4 `dd599c2`, F-20 r2 `0d2e178`, F-21 r3 `1e1ecc7`, F-29 r6 `ef342f3` |
| `v13m` `v33e` | verification, **new trees** | F-13 r5 `224a5b8` and F-33 r4 `648a819` — both delivered at the stoppage and never verified. New slugs because the implementer's tree cannot verify its own work |
| `f08d` `f11e` | rework | F-08 round seven (three blocking), F-11 round nine (five blocking) |
| `f13c` `f33d` | idle | the implementer trees whose rounds are now under verification. Left standing rather than retired, so the round's author is recoverable if a verifier disputes it |

### What was sitting in two of those trees

Before dispatching I read `git status` and `git diff HEAD` in all eleven
surviving worktrees rather than assuming an externally-stopped agent leaves a
clean one. Two did not:

- **`v12j` held a live mutant in production source.** `->orderBy('ip_addresses.address')`
  had been deleted from `HeldQuarantineAddresses::inPool()`, leaving the comment
  beneath it describing a line that was no longer there. That is a deliberate
  breakage from step four of the closure protocol, never restored because the
  agent performing it was stopped mid-measurement.
- **`f11e` held a planted probe *method* in production source** — an
  `f11eProbe()` added to `IpamCollector.php`, calling `saveMany` so that F-11's
  writer-scan would have something to catch. Not a test file: a method on a
  metrics collector.

Both restored, both verified by an empty `git diff` and by reading the restored
region rather than trusting the command's exit status. `v04j` also holds an
untracked `VerifierV04jProbeTest.php` inside the collected test path; I left
that one for its verifier and named it in the dispatch, because a probe in the
collected path perturbs every suite count and the agent needs to decide
knowingly rather than inherit it.

**The reason this is worth a section rather than a line.** A stopped agent's
tree is not a paused tree, it is an abandoned one, and the two edits above were
both in `src/`, both plausible-looking, and both would have been swept into the
next commit by an agent that trusted its own checkout. The mutant is the worse
of the two: it removes a tie-breaker from a quarantine query, which does not
fail any test that does not specifically look for ordering — it just makes the
order non-deterministic. It would have shipped green.

So the rule I have been giving agents — *your own `git status` is the
authority, not the brief and not a file's plausibility* — is not boilerplate,
and this is the second time in this programme that reading it has paid. Every
dispatch above names its tree's specific hazard, by filename, rather than
repeating the general warning.

## All forty-seven are traced, and the count is the smaller half of the news

F-24 was the last one. Every finding in the authorised namespace now has either
a closure with an independent verification behind it, or a read-only trace
against the code on this branch. Nothing in F-01..F-47 is still being taken on
the audit's word alone.

What the tracing changed, aggregated once rather than re-argued per row:

| | |
|---|---|
| Traced findings where the audit's claim held as written | the majority |
| Traced findings where I had to **correct** the audit | F-23 (27 architecture tests → 28), F-25 (headline claim already fixed), F-39 (the alert count), F-47 (three source states → seven), F-24 (limb 3's "never reads the domain" is false), F-38 (five gates named; five sampled, all sound) |
| Traced findings where the tree is **worse** than the audit says | F-23 (the enum list is hand-written: 70 imports against 136 enum files), F-47 (a `retired_at` column nothing writes), F-24 (five simulators the audit never names, and a payment simulator that cannot fail at all) |

The pattern across the corrections is worth naming once. The audit was
**right about the defect and unreliable about the quantifier** — almost every
count in it moved when re-derived, in both directions. That is not a criticism
of the audit; it is the expected result of an audit measuring a tree that is
still being worked. It is a standing instruction for the re-audit: re-derive
every number, and never carry a figure forward because a previous document
published it.

### And a claim of mine that the tree did not support, found by checking it

Writing this section, I went to say "twelve briefs on disk, four more in the
rows" — and checked instead of asserting. Four rows (F-30, F-36, F-37, F-39)
read **brief ready**. `find` across the entire container returns no `f30.md`,
`f36.md`, `f37.md` or `f39.md`, in the scratchpad or anywhere else. The briefs
do not exist.

I cannot establish how that happened — whether the files were written into a
container that was later replaced, or whether I wrote the trace into the ledger
row and then recorded a brief I never separately produced. Both are consistent
with what survives, so the ledger now says only what is established: **brief
file absent — owed before dispatch.** Not "lost", which would be a cause I have
no evidence for.

The mechanism is the same one this program has now hit in several shapes: **the
ledger lives in the repository and the briefs live in the scratchpad, so a
ledger row can outlive the artifact it points at.** A row asserting the
existence of a file is a claim about the tree, and it decays exactly like any
other claim about the tree. Two consequences, both binding on the rest of this
work:

1. A row may say a brief exists only if the file exists **at the moment the row
   is written and in a location that survives the container** — which, for
   anything a future session must read, means the repository.
2. Any dispatch that consumes one of these four rows must write the brief
   first. A round dispatched against "brief ready" with no brief is a round
   dispatched against nothing, and it would have looked, from the ledger,
   exactly like the other ten.

And I applied rule 1 to itself rather than only writing it down: the twelve
briefs that existed are now in the repository at `docs/round-2-briefs/`, and
every reference in this ledger points there instead of at a scratchpad path
that the next container will not have.

**Then I paid the debt rather than recording it.** Rather than leave four rows
reading *owed*, I traced F-30, F-36, F-37 and F-39 myself in the same sitting
and wrote their briefs. All sixteen now exist. The rows below carry what the
tracing found, and three of the four moved the finding:

- **F-36** throws *after* the reconciliation has already succeeded, so the task
  fails every run while doing most of its job — the shape that trains an
  operator to ignore it. The audit's single line does not say this, and it is
  the worse half.
- **F-37**'s second limb is exact: a `Claimed` row has no timeout, no sweeper
  and no operator exit, and the own-transaction commit that makes the claim
  durable is precisely what makes the crash window real. Its first limb needed
  narrowing — dedicated is not unmonitored, it has a collector and a dashboard;
  it is the *power* path that is absent from both.
- **F-39**'s fifteen is correct and, unusually in this audit, survived
  re-derivation unchanged. But the fifteen are not one defect: `QueueBacklog` is
  a truncation of two real alerts with different thresholds and different
  routing, not an invention, and "wrote fifteen rules" would be the wrong
  outcome dressed as success.
- **F-30** produced a false hypothesis of mine, recorded in its row so the round
  does not inherit it: I read the Horizon middleware config as having been
  weakened and it is the package's own default.

The one thing I could not recover is whether the four briefs ever existed. That
stays unestablished, and this section says so rather than guessing.

The generalisation I will not make: this does not mean the four traces are
wrong. The traces are *in the rows*, in the repository, and they survived. What
was lost is the expansion of them, which is recoverable by re-reading the code
the row names.

## Product decisions escalated to the user, and their answers

Only decisions the repository genuinely does not settle, where more than one
contract is defensible and the choice changes what the code must do.

| Decision | Context | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| How a shared-hosting customer supplies the domain their account is built for. | The repository asserts a lifecycle step that needs a domain and provides no way to supply one: `PlaceOrderRequest` has no domain field and `CheckoutLine` carries only `planId`/`quantity`. F-04's literal sentence. | **Ask for it at checkout.** Implemented with the portal, both locales, the capability matrix and OpenAPI in scope. |
| What happens to a running machine or hosting account when its order is refunded in full. | F-19 made `Refunded` reachable for the first time, which turned a dormant sentence in `PlanCapacity`'s docblock — that refunded orders release their unit — into live behaviour. Measured consequence: `order=refunded service=active subscription=active CLAIMED=0`, and the last unit of a finite plan sold twice while the first customer's machine was still running. | **Keep the service, release nothing yet.** A refund records the money and nothing else; the plan unit and the coupon hold come back when the *service* ends, not when money moves. Terminating stays a separate act. `PlanCapacity`'s docblock is wrong as written and is corrected with the code. |

## A safety instruction that named a tool nobody had written

The third coordinator defect of this programme, and the first one an agent hit
rather than I did.

Every worktree this pool has ever produced carries a banner, and the banner has
said since the first one:

> NEVER edit anything under `vendor/` in place. `vendor/<namespace>` here is a
> SYMLINK to the canonical checkout's, so an in-place edit is MACHINE-WIDE for
> its duration, not worktree-local. [...] If you must mutate a package to
> reproduce a runtime condition, run
> `scratchpad/unshare-vendor-package.sh <slug> <namespace>/<package>` first.

**That script did not exist.** Not in the pool directory, not in any worktree,
not anywhere on the box. It had been named in the banner, and repeated by me in
brief after brief, for the whole programme, and nobody had needed it until
F-30's round two needed a mutant in Horizon's own `routes/web.php`.

The shape of the defect is worth naming precisely, because it is not "a missing
file". An agent that reaches a safety instruction and finds no tool has two
options and both are bad: **skip the mutation**, which weakens the round it was
dispatched to prove, or **improvise an unshare over state twelve concurrent
agents are reading**. F-30 took the second and got it exactly right — it
replaced the `vendor/laravel` symlink with a real directory of per-package
symlinks plus a private `cp -a` of `horizon`, mutated only the private copy,
restored by content hash, and put the symlink back. I verified the canonical
tree independently afterwards: inode 780025, sha256 `39cb9e50…`, unmoved. But
that was one agent's care standing in for a mechanism, which is the exact
arrangement §7 exists to remove.

The script is now written, tested, installed into all twelve live worktrees,
and installed by `mkworktree.sh` into every worktree it makes from here. It
gives the named package its own inode, proves the autoloader resolves it inside
the worktree rather than the canonical one, fingerprints the canonical package
before and after every run and aborts if it moved, and its `--restore` refuses
unless the private copy matches canonical byte for byte — because a restore
that discards a live mutation leaves you unable to prove the mutation was ever
undone.

**And the script was wrong on its first run, in a way only the test found.** Its
fingerprint hashed `sha256sum` output over *absolute* paths, so the canonical
digest carried `/home/user/cloud/...` and the private one carried
`/home/user/worktrees/<slug>/...`. The two could never be equal. `--restore`
would have refused **forever**, on a correctly restored package, with a message
telling the agent its mutation was still live. The first agent to meet that
would have gone round the script — and a safety tool that cannot be satisfied is
worse than no safety tool at all, because it teaches people to skip it. I found
it by running the full cycle (unshare, mutate, refuse, un-mutate, restore),
not by reading the code I had just written.

Which is the programme's own third sweep-discipline line pointed back at me: a
gate written after the fix and never seen red. I had written a refusal, watched
it refuse, and very nearly filed that as proof — when the refusal was firing for
a reason unrelated to the thing it was measuring. The corrected script has now
been seen red for the right reason (mutation live, refuses) and green for the
right reason (mutation undone, restores, canonical unmoved).

## The test I now use for whether a reservation blocks

F-23's round two came back **UPHELD WITH RESERVATIONS, zero blocking**, from a
verification I rate among the best in this programme, and I held the finding
open anyway. Overruling a verifier in the *strict* direction is new here — the
recorded precedents run the other way, a verifier overturning me — so the
reasoning had better be a rule rather than a mood.

The rule: **a reservation is blocking when it falsifies a claim the shipped
code makes about itself.**

Not when it finds a hole. Every instrument in this repository has holes and the
good ones say where. Not when the hole is reachable, either — reachability
decides severity, not whether the round closes. The question is narrower and it
is about honesty rather than coverage: *does the code, as delivered, assert
something about its own reach that is not true?*

By that test, F-23's `->value` hole blocks. The shipped docblock says F-47's
decision *"can no longer be taken silently in either direction"*, and a write
spelled `Enum::Case->value` — the spelling query-builder writes are **required**
to use, present at ten production sites — takes it silently. The verifier's two
grounds for non-blocking are both true and neither touches this: that the hole
is inherited from round one says nothing about whether the sentence is true
now, and that no current verdict depends on it says the hole is benign today,
which is a fact about the tree and not about the claim.

And the same test explains why the other three reservations do **not** block.
The nested-literal haystack is disclosed in the docblock; the code does not
claim to cover it. The `array(…)` long form is undisclosed — but the remedy
there is also a sentence, because the defect is that a `T_ARRAY` check
*advertises* coverage it does not deliver, which is the same species one size
down. The closure's wrong cost estimate is a false sentence about performance,
not about reach, and nothing downstream relies on it. Three sentences to fix,
no round to reopen.

This is the same test I applied to F-29's round seven an hour earlier, before I
had named it. There the docblock drew its boundary at *a dynamic callee* while
the implementation drew it at *a `T_STRING` token with a case-sensitive prefix*,
and `\preg_match` fell outside neither exclusion and was skipped anyway. Same
shape, same ruling, and I want the two decided by one rule rather than by two
independent judgements that happened to agree.

The rule has a cost I should name. It makes a round's *docblock* load-bearing in
a way that invites the wrong repair: an implementer can always satisfy it by
narrowing the sentence instead of widening the code. That is exactly §27's
family — closing a finding by rewriting the expectation — so the rule needs its
companion, and here it is: **when the sentence and the code disagree, the code
moves if the property is closed, and the sentence moves only if it is not.**
F-29's callee kinds are a closed grammatical set, so the code moved. F-23's
nested literal is not, so the sentence may.

> **This statement is defective and is superseded.** See *"One word was doing two
> jobs, and I decided two findings opposite ways under it"* below. The sentence
> above is left standing rather than edited because eleven briefs and several
> adjudications were written over it and a reader meeting it in one of those
> needs to find it here. That is the same line round seven of
F-29 drew for itself — *close what a property closes, measure what is left* — and
it is doing a second job now.

## I quoted a sentence that does not exist, twice, in this file

F-37's verifier was asked to check my F-34 ruling rather than re-litigate it. It
accepted the ruling and then caught the ruling's evidence.

Both F-34's row and F-37's rendered the reasoning as a quotation from the
source:

> `ReleaseQuarantinedAddresses` skips exactly those rows because *"a clock
> answers none of the question the timeout asks"*.

**That sentence appears nowhere in this repository.** I checked before accepting
the correction, because an accusation against my own canonical document
deserves the same treatment as any other claim: `grep` for it across every
`.php` and `.md` file returns my two ledger rows and nothing else.

What the code actually says is two sentences, in two files:

* `ReleaseReason.php:96` — *"A timeout is not a waiting period, because time
  answers none of its question."*
* `ReleaseQuarantinedAddresses.php:48` — *"A timeout quarantine is not a waiting
  period and does not end on a clock."*

My version is a faithful paraphrase. It says nothing the code does not say, the
ruling built on it is unaffected, and the verifier confirmed the substance
independently: `requiresOperatorClearance()` is true for `ProvisioningTimedOut`
alone, the exclusion is deliberate, and the enum's docblock carries the two
outcomes with opposite consequences that make a clock the wrong instrument.

None of which is the point. **A paraphrase in quotation marks is a false
sentence about the tree**, and this programme's entire subject is sentences
about the tree that do not survive being checked. I have rejected two rounds
this week for a docblock claiming reach its implementation did not have. The
species is identical and the fact that mine was in prose rather than in a
guard makes it worse, not better: a guard's false claim at least has a test
beside it that somebody might run, and a ledger's has only a reader who trusts
it. Both quotations are now the real sentences, with their file and line.

Two things follow that are worth more than the correction.

**It did not survive one grep, and nobody had run the grep.** The phrase sat in
the canonical document through every wave, was copied from the row into a brief,
and was then handed to an agent as evidence. The cost was not paid here only
because the paraphrase happened to be accurate. `validate-ledger-rows.py`
catches a row that advertises a round its narrative never records; it cannot
catch a row that quotes a sentence the source never wrote. That is a second
mechanical check this file could have, and I am recording the gap rather than
building it mid-wave — a quotation gate written now, over a document I am
editing in every commit, is a gate I would be tempted to shape around whatever
it flags.

**It is the third time a verifier has corrected my own writing rather than the
round's**, after the F-15 brief that described the wrong round and the Pint note
that was off by one file. The pattern is consistent enough to name: my errors
are in the *evidence layer* — a figure, a line citation, a quotation — and not
in the rulings those artefacts support. That is the layer nobody is dispatched
to check, because every brief points agents at the code. So the instruction is
now in the briefs themselves: **check every sentence I have written against the
tree before relying on it.**

## The shared vendor tree moved, and the filesystem kept the receipt

F-30's verifier found forensic evidence that the canonical, machine-wide
`vendor/laravel/horizon/routes/web.php` was **written in place** during round
two's working window — contradicting that round's statement that the canonical
tree did not move. I reproduced the whole finding before acting on it.

```
inode  780025    links 1
birth  2026-09-19 13:11:45      (install)
mtime  2026-09-25 11:01:32.568032344
ctime  2026-09-25 11:01:32.568032344
parent dir routes/ mtime  2026-09-19 13:11:45   (unchanged)

mtime distribution across the package's 324 files:
  323  2026-09-19 13:11
    1  2026-09-25 11:01      <- routes/web.php, the file V7 mutated
```

The inode is unchanged, the birth time is unchanged, and **the parent
directory's mtime is unchanged**, which rules out replacement by `mv`, by
`sed -i`, or by delete-and-recreate. The file was opened and truncated through
its existing inode: a `>` redirection, a plain `cp` onto the target, or a
`file_put_contents`. Round one's commits are at 09:27 and 09:29 and round two's
is at 11:11, so 11:01:32 falls inside round two's window and nowhere near
anything else.

**What is not in doubt: the content is clean.** The verifier checked it against
a baseline nobody else had used — a bare clone of laravel/horizon sitting in
composer's VCS cache — and I repeated that independently against the version in
`composer.lock`:

```
v5.48.3:routes/web.php     39cb9e507dc5e2d3e95e91777b5c2b62ec7a1b4598173a584a32c0a9ea428e50
vendor/.../routes/web.php  39cb9e507dc5e2d3e95e91777b5c2b62ec7a1b4598173a584a32c0a9ea428e50
```

Byte-identical to upstream. That baseline is worth more than the hash I took at
the time, because my hash only said the file matched what I had just seen; this
one says it matches what Laravel shipped, and it could not be forged without
also rewriting the bare clone.

### The blast radius, which is the only question that mattered

Twelve other agents were reading that inode. `mtime` records only the **last**
write, so I cannot see when the mutation landed, how long it was live, or
whether there was an earlier one — and I have said so rather than reconstructing
a window I cannot measure.

What I could do is bound the damage by asking what in this repository could
possibly have observed the mutation that was described: a change of HTTP verb on
`/horizon/jobs/silenced`, `GET` to `POST`. Seven test files in the tree
enumerate routes. Every one of them is blind to it:

* `EveryAuthenticatedRouteIsThrottledTest` filters to `str_starts_with($route->uri(), 'api/')`;
* `AdminRoutesRequireAPermissionTest` filters to `api/admin`;
* `OneThrottleBucketPerVerbTest` iterates everything but collects only routes
  whose middleware starts with `throttle:`, and Horizon carries no throttle —
  which is a fact this very finding established;
* `EveryControllerMethodIsReachableTest` checks that a route's controller class
  exists, which a verb change does not touch.

Horizon's routes match none of those filters. The only assertion in the
repository sensitive to that route's verb is F-30's own verb map, which is new
in round two and therefore existed on no other branch during the window. And
`assertCount(22)`, the pin that *does* exist elsewhere, is blind to a verb
change by construction — which is the thing round two proved on purpose.

So: **no other agent's published figure is impeached by this, on the evidence
available.** One more thing points the same way: an in-place write through `>`
truncates before it writes, so a suite booting during that instant would take a
parse error, not a quiet wrong answer. The failure mode is loud.

The limit of that conclusion is exact and I will not overstate it: it holds for
*a verb change*, because a verb change is the only mutation anyone has
described. A different write to that file in an unobserved earlier moment would
need its own analysis, and no evidence of one exists either way.

### What I actually take from it

Not that an agent was careless. That agent restored the file, verified it by
content hash, reported the mechanism it had improvised, and its work is upheld.
It is the third agent in this programme to do something exactly right that the
toolchain should never have asked it to do by hand.

The lesson is about **what a content hash can and cannot certify.** The round
proved the bytes were back. That is true and it was checked honestly. It says
nothing at all about whether the bytes were ever gone, and the ledger's sentence
*"canonical unchanged"* silently promised the second while evidencing only the
first. Every agent in this programme, me included, has been treating a matching
hash as proof that nothing happened, when it is only proof of where things
ended. The filesystem kept a record we were not reading.

Two changes follow. `unshare-vendor-package.sh` — which did not exist when this
happened, and whose absence is what forced the improvisation — now fingerprints
the canonical package before and after every run and aborts if it moved; I have
added nothing to it here, because the correct tool was already the answer and
the incident is its justification rather than a new requirement. And the
standing instruction to agents gains a line: **when you report that a shared
file is unchanged, say whether you are claiming it never moved or only that it
ended where it started**, because those are different claims and only one of
them is provable by a hash taken at the end.

## A clause a verifier proposed for my blocking test, and what I did with it

F-39's verifier applied my standard — *a reservation is blocking when it
falsifies a claim the shipped code makes about itself* — said where it had used
it, and then proposed an addition:

> a reservation should also block when the evidence offered for a claim does not
> support it, even if the claim is true.

It is a good instinct and it is aimed at a real thing. Its own worked example is
R2: the round claimed a widened citation threshold would be self-detecting, and
the verifier showed that holds only at the value the round happened to pick —
`MIN_CITATION_LENGTH = 20` leaves the gate green while ignoring every alert name
under twenty characters. The claim about the gate's soundness is true; the
mutation offered as proof of it does not prove it.

**I am not taking it as a blocking criterion, and I am taking it as something
else.** Note first that its author applied it and it changed no outcome: R2
still did not block, because the gate underneath is sound. A criterion that
fires and then defers is not deciding anything.

The deeper reason is that the two tests answer different questions. *Does the
code lie about itself?* is a question about the artefact being shipped, and the
artefact outlives every one of us — a false docblock misleads the next reader
whether or not anybody here noticed. *Is the proof weaker than advertised?* is a
question about the **record**, and the record is correctable in place, by the
ledger, today. Blocking a round to fix its own report is the wrong instrument:
it sends an agent back to re-do work that was correct, when the thing that needs
changing is a paragraph I can write myself.

So it becomes a **reporting obligation rather than a gate**. In this programme
the ledger is a deliverable in its own right, so an oversold proof damages
something real — it just damages the document, not the code. The rule:

> When a verification finds that a round's evidence does not support a claim the
> round made, the claim's status is downgraded **in the ledger**, in the round's
> own row, naming what was actually proved. The round does not reopen unless the
> claim itself is false.

R2 is recorded that way in F-39's row: the threshold's defence is described as
what the mutation actually establishes, and the one-assertion remedy is named
rather than demanded.

There is one boundary worth stating, because it is where the two tests touch. If
the oversold evidence is itself *in the shipped artefact* — a docblock that says
"pinned by the mutation below" where the mutation pins something narrower — then
the code does lie about itself, and the first test fires normally. What the new
clause covers is only the case where the overselling lives in a hand-back or a
commit message, which is to say in the record.

## The session scratchpad is shared, and it nearly handed a verifier somebody else's number

F-04's verifier began its bands and found, already sitting in the scratchpad it
had been given, a file called `band3.out`, timestamped before it started and
reading `tests:4090` — **round seven's own output, the very figure the verifier
was there to check independently.** It noticed, copied its artefacts into a
private subdirectory, and re-derived every number from files it had written
itself.

The cause is mine. `/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-cloud/<uuid>/scratchpad` is this
session's scratchpad, and *this session* includes every agent I dispatch: it
currently holds roughly two hundred files from something like forty agents, with
directories named `f08e/`, `v11v/`, `v23b/`, `f14e/` sitting beside loose output
files owned by nobody in particular. `mkworktree.sh` has always created a
private `/tmp/claude-0/agent-<slug>/` and the banner has always named it as
`scratch`, but the shared path is what agents actually reach for, because it is
the one the harness tells them about.

The failure this sets up is the sweep family's purest form: **a file whose name
describes what you are measuring, containing a number that is right, produced by
the run you are supposed to be checking independently.** Nothing about it looks
wrong. An implementer's band output and its verifier's band output have the same
shape, the same filename and often the same value — and the one case where the
value would differ is exactly the case where the verification matters.

What makes it worse than an ordinary collision is that it defeats the *purpose*
of independence rather than the *mechanics* of it. The worktrees are isolated,
the databases are isolated, the Redis indexes are isolated — and then the
evidence lands in one drawer.

I have not built a mechanism for this, and I want to be honest about why rather
than dress it up: the fix that would actually work is making each agent's
scratch path the only one it is told about, and I cannot change what the harness
hands a subagent. So the remedy is instruction, which is the weaker kind, and it
now goes in every brief: **write measurement artefacts to
`/tmp/claude-0/agent-<slug>/`, and if you read a file you did not write in this
round, say so.** That second clause is the part that matters, because it turns a
silent contamination into a reportable one.

Worth recording that the verifier caught this unprompted, and that it is the
second time in this programme an agent has found a measurement hazard in the
toolchain I gave it rather than in the work it was sent to do.

## A sixth line for the sweep discipline, and the first one that is red rather than green

Every previous member of this family reports **success** for a reason unrelated
to the thing being measured: a suite that ran zero tests, a filter that matched
nothing, a gate written after the fix, a guard reimplementing a framework's
resolution, `numstat` blind to a new file. F-23's round three found the mirror
image, in itself, and reported it:

> My first (a)/(b) run was a false green-equivalent of exactly the family the
> brief names. I wrote the haystack mutation in `perl` inside an unquoted
> heredoc; `$job` was interpolated away, the substitution never matched, and all
> four cells came back red — red for a reason unrelated to the thing being
> measured.

So the sixth line is: **a mutation that did not land produces a red that looks
exactly like a kill.**

It belongs in the family and it is worse than its siblings, for one reason that
took me a moment to see. Everything else in this programme is organised around
distrusting green. A green result gets three proofs, a JUnit check and a
skipped-count; nobody signs off a green without asking what else could have
produced it. **Red gets none of that**, because red is what you were hoping for.
In a mutation campaign the red *is* the deliverable — it is the sentence "this
guard catches that defect" — and a mutation that silently failed to apply hands
you that sentence for free, for every mutant, forever. A campaign of twenty
mutants could report twenty kills and have proved nothing at all, and every
individual line of its table would look right.

What caught it was the landing proof, and only barely: the implementer says its
own grep had filtered the relevant line out and it found the problem by going
back and reading the raw output. That is the same margin as the other near-misses
in this programme — a person choosing to look at something they had already
mechanically "checked".

The mechanical answer is small and it is now the standard for every mutation in
this programme: **the mutator must assert its own effect**, in code, at the
moment of writing —

```python
assert out != s, "MUTATION DID NOT LAND"
```

— and the result of a run whose mutation did not land is not a kill, not a
survivor, and not a data point. It is a failed measurement, and it is re-run.

Note what this does *not* replace. `git status --porcelain` proves a file
changed; it cannot prove the change is the one you meant, and a heredoc that
mangles a variable can still produce a diff if it substitutes something. The
assert above is about the edit; the content hash is about the file; and reading
the mutated region with your own eyes is about neither. This round did all three
in the end, which is why it has a result worth reading.

**And a smaller note about me.** `validate-ledger-rows.py` has now caught me
three times in one day, always the same way: I write a row's narrative, advertise
the verification worktree in the status cell, and never name it in the prose. The
gate is not finding a different defect each time — it is finding the same habit
of mine, which is that I treat the status cell as the live field and the
narrative as history. That is precisely the reading the gate was written to
break, and it turns out the reader it most needed to break was its author.

## 191 branches this programme has produced, and CI has built none of them

F-38's round found this and correctly refused to touch it. I measured it myself
before recording it:

```
$ sed -n '/^on:/,/workflow_dispatch/p' .github/workflows/ci.yml
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main, 'claude/**']
  workflow_dispatch:

remediation/   191        <- measured when this section was written; 199 a few hours later
claude/          2
```

Every branch a remediation agent produces is pushed and never built. Only
`pull_request` and `workflow_dispatch` would reach CI for them, and this
programme opens no pull requests.

**It is smaller than it first reads, and I want to be precise rather than
alarming about it.** The integration branch is `claude/relaxed-turing-nh8ybf`,
which matches `claude/**`, so §9's eighth step — exact-sha CI — does run where
it is specified to run, on the branch things are integrated into. Agent branches
are not meant to be built: each round runs the gates locally and hands back the
output, and thirteen concurrent CI runs of a full matrix would be a worse
arrangement than the one we have.

What is actually wrong is smaller and is a documentation defect of the kind this
programme keeps finding. The trigger carries a comment justifying itself:

> a branch that is pushed but never opened as a PR — which is how this
> repository has been worked — was never built at all.

That reasoning was true when `claude/**` was the working convention. The
convention then moved to `remediation/**` and the filter did not, so the comment
now describes a protection the filter no longer provides for 191 of 193
branches. The sentence and the code disagree, and by the standing rule the
question is whether the property is closed: it is not — building 191 branches on
every push is not a thing anyone wants — **so the sentence moves, not the code.**

I have not changed either. Changing the filter would start builds for 191
branches while thirteen agents are live, and the honest fix is one comment,
which belongs with the integration work rather than in the middle of a wave.
Recorded here so that whoever does it does not instead "fix" the filter.

## Porcelain is quiet in one direction, and that is a landing proof failing

The fifth discipline line says `git diff --numstat` is blind to a file that is
new, so `git status --porcelain` is the authority for whether a mutation landed.
F-40's round found the other edge of the same instrument, and it is worth having
because it points the opposite way.

Two of its mutations **restored HEAD content** — reinstating a sentence that the
round's own commit had deleted, to check that the new gate reddens on it. For
those, `git status --porcelain` did not get louder. It went **quiet**: the file
now matched HEAD, so porcelain correctly reported nothing, and a harness reading
porcelain as "did my edit land?" would have concluded that it had not.

The distinction, which I had never had to state:

> **Porcelain is the authority on difference-from-HEAD. It is not an authority
> on "something changed since a moment ago".**

For every mutation that moves *away* from the committed text, those two
questions have the same answer and porcelain is the right instrument. For a
mutation that moves *towards* it, they have opposite answers, and only
`sha256sum` against the value taken immediately before the edit can tell you
what happened.

This matters more than it looks, because the mutations that restore committed
text are not exotic. They are exactly the ones you write when a round has just
*fixed* a false sentence and you want to prove the new gate catches it coming
back — which is to say, they are the standard shape of a deliberate-breakage
test for a documentation fix. Every round in this programme that repairs a
docblock and then proves the repair is pinned will write one.

Combined with the sixth line found this week — a mutation that did not land
produces a red that looks exactly like a kill — the rule for the whole family is
now one sentence: **take a hash before, take a hash after, and compare those two
to each other rather than either of them to HEAD.**

## The sixth line has a twin, and the landing assert is not enough

Two verifications this week added to the mutation-discipline family, and between
them they finish it.

**A scan that did not land produces a green that looks exactly like a pass.**
F-40's verifier built an instrument to count invisible cross-module references
and it reported **zero** — a clean result, agreeing with nothing, because its
string tokeniser mis-parses any file containing apostrophes in prose comments,
and `ReferenceTopologyValidator` has **221** of them. It found the fault only
because it checked a known positive first. It committed the broken instrument
alongside the corrected one, labelled, as evidence.

That is the read-direction twin of the sixth line, and the verifier's own
framing is right: it is **worse** than the red case, because you were hoping for
green. A mutation that fails to land at least produces a result you have to
explain; a scan that fails to parse produces the result you wanted.

**And the landing assert is necessary but not sufficient.** F-29's verifier ran
a mutation harness that correctly refused to proceed unless the anchor occurred
exactly once, the file hash moved, and the new text read back — and it still got
six cells of meaningless red, because *the mutation landed on the wrong line*.
My brief had mis-located the site; the mutant it produced inverted the policy so
that it refused every ordinary host. All six cells came back red at an identical
assertion count, including two the brief specified must be green.

What caught it was not the harness. It was two cross-checks the harness cannot
make: **the uniformity of a figure across cells that should differ**, and **a
cell being red that was specified green**. Its conclusion, which I am adopting:

> The mutant must also be shown not to change behaviour the row measures for
> other reasons.

So the discipline for a mutation is now four things, not one. The edit must be
proved to have happened (hash before ≠ hash after). It must be proved to have
happened **where you meant** (read the mutated region). It must be proved
**behaviour-preserving except for the property under test** — which for a
guard-mutation usually means the mutant and the control must differ in the cells
that should differ. And the restore must be proved by hash against the value
taken before, not against HEAD.

Three of those four exist because an agent here was burned by the missing one.
The fourth — reading the mutated region — is the one I have been asking for
since the fifth stoppage, and it is the one that would have caught this too.

## The third face: a mutation that did not land reads as a survivor

The family now has three orientations and F-34's round found the one that was
missing.

- **False red.** A mutation that did not land produces a red that looks exactly
  like a kill. (F-23's `perl`-in-an-unquoted-heredoc.)
- **False green.** A scan that did not land produces a pass that looks exactly
  like a clean tree. (F-40's tokeniser, choked on 221 apostrophes.)
- **False survivor.** A mutation that did not land, in a campaign where you
  *expect* a kill, reads as a **survivor** — and sends you hunting for a hole
  that is not there.

The third one happened like this. A mutant's literal matched **zero** times. The
harness did the right thing and refused to write anything. But the test run went
ahead regardless — against the **unmutated** file — and came back `passed`. In a
mutation table, `passed` in the result column next to a mutation's name is
indistinguishable from a real survivor.

What makes this worse than the other two is where the cost lands. A false red
wastes a verdict; a false green wastes a guarantee. A **false survivor wastes
attention in the most expensive direction available**: it is a specific,
credible, apparently-measured claim that the guard has a hole, and the honest
response to it is to go and look for the hole. The round caught it only because
its mutator asserted its own effect and it read the abort message rather than
the result table.

So the obligation is not only that a mutator asserts its own landing. It is that
**a harness which refuses to mutate must also refuse to run**, and that a run
which happened anyway is not a data point in either direction — not a kill, not
a survivor, not evidence of coverage and not evidence of a gap. The rule for the
whole family, in one line: *take a hash before, take a hash after, compare those
two to each other, and if they are equal then nothing you measure next means
anything.*


## The correction to the provisioner was itself a program, and it broke the pool for a minute

F-41's round one falsified the reason this document and `scratchpad/mkworktree.sh`
had both been giving for why the thirteen-worktree pool is isolated. Correcting
the two places was the obvious follow-up and it is written up in the F-41 row.
What is worth recording separately is what happened when I corrected the second
one.

The provisioner's banner — the text every agent reads on arrival — is emitted
from an **unquoted heredoc**, and the script runs under `set -u`. My replacement
paragraph is about `$_SERVER` and `$_ENV`, because that is what the real
mechanism is about. The shell expanded them, found nothing, and the script died:

```
Preparing worktree (new branch 'remediation/v41b')
mkworktree.sh: line 234: _ENV: unbound variable
```

It died **after** creating the worktree, the database, the Redis slot and the
autoloader check, and **before** printing a single line of the banner. So the
worktree was fully and correctly provisioned, and an agent handed it would have
received none of the instructions — not the ledger warning, not the `git stash`
warning, not the vendor-unshare tool, not the Redis index it was allocated. A
silent, complete, unusable provision. I verified the four components by hand and
re-ran the escape rather than re-running the script, because a re-run would have
dropped and recreated a database that by then existed.

Three things in this that are not about shell quoting.

**A document that is also a program has two readers, and I was writing for one
of them.** The banner is prose to the agent and source to bash. Every other
correction I have made in this programme has been to a file with one reader.
This one needed to be right in two languages simultaneously and I checked it in
neither — I checked it against the *facts*, which were correct, and shipped it.

**The failure mode is the family this ledger keeps recording, inverted.** The
sweep-discipline lines are all about an instrument that reports success for a
reason unrelated to what it measured. This is an instrument that reported
nothing at all while its subject was in perfect condition, and the only reason I
noticed is that the exit status was non-zero and I was watching. Had the banner
been emitted before the provisioning rather than after, the same bug would have
produced a *half-built* worktree with a *complete* banner, which is the strictly
worse arrangement and is the one most scripts have.

**And the smallest fact is the one I would most like to remember.** The
paragraph I was inserting exists because a round proved that a mechanism I had
asserted eleven times was not the mechanism. The correction to that assertion
then failed for a reason entirely unrelated to whether it was true. Being right
about the content is not the same as the content arriving, and I have now made
the coordinator-level version of that mistake four times: a tool named in a
banner that did not exist, a relative path that resolved elsewhere for an agent,
a scratchpad shared between agents that handed one of them another's figures,
and now a paragraph that was accurate and unprintable.

## The migration collisions are resolved, on paper, and the convention was already in the tree

This has sat as "renumber six colliding migrations at integration" for most of
round two. With nine agents in flight and nothing dispatchable, I worked it out.
Three corrections and a plan.

**It is seven files, not six, in three groups.** Across all 191 remediation
branches there are ten migrations that the integration branch does not have.
Three of them are uncontested — F-32's `2026_04_15_000032_index_hosting_packages_by_plan`
and F-04's `2026_04_24_000000_one_live_hosting_account_per_domain` and
`2026_04_26_000000_a_hosting_account_serves_a_canonical_name`. The other seven
collide:

| timestamp | finding | migration | table |
|---|---|---|---|
| `2026_04_15_000000` | F-04 | `record_the_domain_a_hosting_line_was_bought_for` | `order_items` |
| `2026_04_15_000000` | F-08 | `record_which_payment_failure_the_dunning_counter_counted` | `subscriptions` |
| `2026_04_15_000000` | F-15 | `reserve_a_provider_identity_before_the_call` | `provisioning_jobs` |
| `2026_04_16_000000` | F-11 | `record_which_call_left_a_dns_record_unanswered` | `dns_records` |
| `2026_04_16_000000` | F-15 | `record_which_cluster_an_identity_was_reserved_against` | `provisioning_jobs` |
| `2026_04_17_000000` | F-11 | `one_live_row_per_provider_record` | `dns_records` |
| `2026_04_17_000000` | F-15 | `record_every_name_a_reserved_identity_was_called_with` | `provisioning_jobs` |

**Why they all landed on the same day is not carelessness.** The integration
branch's last migration is `2026_04_14_000000`. Every branch took the next free
day, independently and correctly, and three of them took it at the same instant
because nobody can see anybody else's branch. This is the isolation working as
designed producing a collision as a direct consequence, which is worth saying
plainly: the collisions are the *price* of §7, not a failure of it.

**Ordering is semantic within two findings and free between all of them.** F-15
has three migrations and all three alter `provisioning_jobs`; F-11 has two and
both alter `dns_records`. So each finding's internal order must survive the
renumbering. Across findings, no two share a table, so their relative order is
unconstrained.

**The convention already exists, and F-32 invented it.** `2026_04_15_000032` is
F-32's migration on F-32's day with F-32's number in the time field. Nobody
wrote that down; it is simply what F-32 did. Following it costs nothing and
invents nothing:

```
2026_04_15_000000_record_the_domain_a_hosting_line_was_bought_for   → 2026_04_15_000004_…
2026_04_15_000000_record_which_payment_failure_the_dunning_counter… → 2026_04_15_000008_…
2026_04_15_000000_reserve_a_provider_identity_before_the_call       → 2026_04_15_000015_…
2026_04_16_000000_record_which_call_left_a_dns_record_unanswered    → 2026_04_16_000011_…
```
