```
2026_04_16_000000_record_which_cluster_an_identity_was_reserved…    → 2026_04_16_000015_…
2026_04_17_000000_one_live_row_per_provider_record                  → 2026_04_17_000011_…
2026_04_17_000000_record_every_name_a_reserved_identity_was_called… → 2026_04_17_000015_…
```

F-11's pair stays `04_16 < 04_17`; F-15's three stay `04_15 < 04_16 < 04_17`.
Both orders are preserved by construction rather than by my checking them, which
is the property to want.

**It is a pure rename.** All seven are `return new class extends Migration`, so
there is no class name to follow the file, and `git grep -F` on each stem across
its own branch outside `database/migrations/` returns **zero** references in
every case. `git mv` and nothing else. The one caveat is that Laravel records
the *filename* in the `migrations` table, so renaming after a run would re-run
the migration — irrelevant here, because integration measures against
`migrate:fresh` databases, but it is the reason this must not be done casually
against a long-lived database.

### And the check I used to build this table was blind to one of the seven

I derived the table column by grepping each migration for `Schema::create`,
`Schema::table` and `->on(`. Six of the seven answered. F-11's
`one_live_row_per_provider_record` came back **empty**, and I nearly recorded it
as touching nothing.

It touches `dns_records`, through `DB::statement` with a heredoc containing
`CREATE UNIQUE INDEX dns_records_one_live_provider_record` — a partial unique
index, which the schema builder cannot express, which is precisely why it is
written as raw SQL. A migration that needs raw SQL is, by definition, the one
doing something the ordinary grammar cannot say, and so it is exactly the
migration most likely to matter and least likely to be seen.

Put that next to the other entries in the sweep-discipline family. This is not a
scan that failed to land or a filter that matched nothing; it is a scan that
landed, ran correctly, and returned an honest empty result for a real subject,
because the subject speaks a second language. The instrument was not broken. It
was **complete for the grammar it knew**, and its silence about the rest was
indistinguishable from an absence. Had F-11's raw index been on
`provisioning_jobs` instead of `dns_records`, my "no two findings share a table,
so the order is free" conclusion would have been wrong, and it would have been
wrong for a reason no amount of re-running the same grep could have surfaced.

## The F-22 × F-39 merge artefact, actually performed — and my warning about it was wrong

This has sat as a prediction since F-39 closed: *"expect `validate-runbook-alerts.py` to go red at the F-22 × F-39 merge — do not fix by deleting the register row."* With the pool full I stopped predicting it and did it, in a throwaway worktree off the integration tip, merging F-22's closed tip `44d0f6f` and then F-39's `64feace`.

**The prediction was right about the collision and wrong about the remedy.**

F-22 merges clean. F-39 then conflicts, textually, in one file: `docs/runbooks/drift.md`. The two findings had resolved the same defect in **opposite directions**, neither able to see the other:

- F-39 found `` `ResourceDriftOpen` `` cited in the runbook and defined in no rule file. Its round ruled — correctly, and with `git log` evidence that no alert had ever been removed — that the name was never real, refused to invent a threshold nobody has watched fire, **removed the citation**, and wrote *"No alert fires for open drift: `lynomia_resource_drift_open` is exported and no rule reads it."* It then listed the gap in `README.md` under *"Pages with no alert here"*, where its own gate checks the list against the rules so it cannot quietly become untrue.
- F-22 **wrote the rule** — `ResourceDriftOpen` and `DriftQueueUnworked` — and expanded the same runbook section to explain when each fires and which one acknowledging clears.

Both are right on their own branch. Merged, F-39's sentence becomes false, so the resolution is F-22's side, and the whole thing then closes in three edits:

```
git checkout --ours docs/runbooks/drift.md          # F-22's text; the alert now exists
python3 infrastructure/scripts/validate-runbook-alerts.py --write
<delete one row from "Pages with no alert here">
```

after which the gate exits 0, and `validate-monitoring.py` and `validate-runbooks.py` are green alongside it.

**And the register row is the part I got wrong.** My warning assumed the collision would tempt somebody to delete a register row to silence a true finding. The opposite is the case: the row reads *"`drift.md` — **Gap.** `lynomia_resource_drift_open` is exported and no rule reads it"*, and F-22 made that sentence false. Deleting it **is** the correct fix, and the gate demands it in those words — *"which is no longer a page no alert names. Remove the row."* A warning written from a prediction, against a merge nobody had performed, told the integrator to preserve a falsehood. It is corrected here and struck where it stands in the F-39 row.

**Two things about F-39's gate that only the merge could show, and both are to its credit.**

It **derives** rather than asserts. The counts block goes from *"64 alerts … 46 … name a page … 9 pages … not named by any alert"* to *"66 … 48 … 8"* with no number typed by a human, which is exactly what F-39's brief demanded (*"fix it by deriving the number rather than editing 55 to 64: a hand-written count in prose is what produced this defect and re-writing it by hand reproduces it"*). Two alerts arriving from an unrelated finding on an unrelated branch are absorbed without anybody noticing they needed to be.

And `--write` **refuses to do the second edit**. It rewrites the derived block and then fails again, still naming the stale row. That is a well-drawn line rather than an incompleteness: a count is a fact about the tree and a machine may recompute it, but a row in *"Pages with no alert here"* carries a human's claim about **why** there is no alert, and a script that silently deleted such a row would be deciding that the claim had stopped mattering. It makes the person do it. Every other self-writing gate in this repository should be read against that boundary.

## One word was doing two jobs, and I decided two findings opposite ways under it

F-38's round-two verifier read my companion rule, found it inconsistent with how
I had just applied it, and said so:

> *"Your companion rule is stated inverted relative to the programme's own
> usage, and it is the rule you asked me to apply. … Property closed ⇒ the
> **sentence** moves. I applied the programme's usage, and it is what carries my
> blocking judgement."*

It is right that something is wrong and right to refuse to guess which way I
meant it. It is not right that the rule is inverted, and the truth is worse than
an inversion, so let me set it out properly rather than accept the easier
diagnosis.

**The rule as written is self-consistent with its own two worked examples.** It
says the code moves if the property is closed, and illustrates: *"F-29's callee
kinds are a closed grammatical set, so the code moved. F-23's nested literal is
not, so the sentence may."* There **closed** means *a closed set* — enumerable,
bounded, fully specifiable. A closed set can be covered, so cover it; an open
one cannot, so narrow the claim. On that reading the rule is correct and the
examples fit.

**But that is not what I have been meaning by it lately.** In F-47 I wrote that
the property is open *because nothing in production writes the state*, and
concluded the sentence moves. In F-34 I wrote that the property is not closed
*because the verifier reached the bad case by construction*, and concluded the
code moves. Those two use **closed** to mean *the claim currently holds* — a
statement about the state of the world, not about the shape of the set. And they
point opposite ways under one sentence. F-38's round two used the second reading
too and I endorsed it in the same brief that shipped the first.

So the word was doing two jobs, and I did not notice because **both readings gave
me the right answer every time** — each case happened to be decidable on whichever
axis I reached for. That is the most dangerous way for a rule to be wrong. A rule
that misfires gets caught by its first bad verdict; a rule that is ambiguous and
lucky accumulates a record of correct decisions that cannot be used to check it.

### The replacement, which asks two questions instead of one

They are independent and both are needed.

**1. Does the code currently satisfy the claim the sentence makes?**
If yes, the sentence is simply describing the wrong thing and the *sentence*
moves. If no, go to question 2.

**2. Is the claim achievable — is the behaviour it names a bounded, specifiable
set?**
If yes, the gap is closeable and the *code* moves. If no — every wrong phrasing,
every dynamic callee, an unbounded blacklist — then no implementation can deliver
the claim and the *sentence* moves, narrowed to what the code can hold.

**And a claim of reach that fails question 1 and passes question 2 is blocking.**
That is the whole of it: shipped code asserting a guarantee it does not provide,
where providing it is possible. Everything else is a correction.

### The four recent adjudications, re-decided under the two questions

Every one comes out the same way, which is the point of writing it down rather
than a reason not to.

- **F-47.** Two distinct claims, which is why one word could not settle it. *"No
  production code enters this state"* passes question 1 — nothing does, by any of
  the four routes the verifier tried — so that sentence stands. *"The state cannot
  acquire a writer while the declaration says it has none"* fails question 1 (a
  raw `'retired'` scalar in a reachable production action passes the whole band)
  and passes question 2 (widen the classifier to the backing scalar and to
  argument position). **Blocking.** As dispatched.
- **F-34.** The docblock says an address held for the platform belongs to no
  customer; the query walks past a customer-less reservation to an older cycle.
  Fails 1, passes 2 — the fix is one clause. **Blocking.** As dispatched, and the
  overrule stands on firmer ground than I gave it.
- **F-38 item 2.** The guard covers all 37 files regardless of what schedules
  them, so the claim holds: passes question 1, sentence moves. Correct as ruled.
- **F-23's nested literal.** Fails 1; fails 2, because the set of nested literal
  shapes is not enumerable. Sentence moves, narrowed. Correct as ruled.

### What this costs, and what it does not

It does not reopen anything. Four adjudications re-decided identically is not a
formality — it is the evidence that the *decisions* were sound and only their
*justification* was ambiguous, which is precisely the ledger-downgrade case this
document already has a clause for. The rule is downgraded; no round reopens.

**And the mechanism deserves its own sentence, because it is the fifth
coordinator defect of one family.** The rule was never written into a brief
*file*. `grep -rl 'property is closed' docs/round-2-briefs/` returns nothing: it
existed only in the dispatch prose I composed for each agent, retyped from
memory eleven times. A load-bearing rule with no single source has nothing to
correct and nothing to diff against, so its two readings could coexist for
eleven dispatches without ever being seen side by side. It now lives in
`docs/round-2-briefs/adjudication-rule.md`, with its worked examples and with
the superseded form printed so an agent meeting the old sentence in an older
brief can recognise it. Every dispatch from here quotes that file rather than
restating it — which is the same repair as deriving a count instead of typing
it, one level up.

What it does cost is the briefs. The defective sentence went out in eleven of
them and in several adjudications, and a verifier that took it literally would
have reached the opposite verdict — this one nearly did, and only refused
because it checked the rule against my own application of it rather than
applying it as written. That is the second time in this programme an agent has
caught a coordinator-level defect by declining to follow an instruction that did
not cohere, and both times the instruction was mine. I would rather record that
than the near miss.

## F-04's cure reintroduces F-24's disease, and it will look exactly like a pass

The sharpest thing F-24's verifier found is not in F-24. It is a cross-branch
interaction that neither finding can see from its own branch, and it is recorded
here with an owner because the merge that creates it will look like a success.

`WhatAGoldenPathMustNotDoTest` plants two canaries —
`PANEL_CANARY = 'Pnl-canary-7f3a9c2e51'` and
`ADMIN_CANARY = 'Wp-canary-b4d8e1f062'` — in a job payload, and then asserts at
lines 109–110 and 125–126 that neither appears on the queue or anywhere a person
could read afterwards.

**`RedactedJsonCast` destroys both canaries at the moment of the write.** They
were never on the queue and never in the row. The assertions were true for a
reason that has nothing to do with the platform's discretion, which is the
purest instance of F-24's own defect in the tree — a security test whose canary
is annihilated before it travels — and it is not among the three limbs the audit
named.

That much is F-24 exposing an existing vacuity, and F-24's limb-3 guard turns it
red, which is correct. **The hazard is what happens next.** F-04's landed repair
has `CreateHostingAccountHandler` mint its own password and ignore the payload
entirely. Measured under an F-04 probe, this test goes **green** — with
`PANEL_CANARY` now unable to reach the provider *by construction*. So one of the
seven reds that F-04 "clears" is cleared by returning the test to vacuity, and
at merge it will be indistinguishable from the other six.

**Owner: whoever integrates F-04.** The fix is to re-point the test at the
minted credential rather than at a payload one. It is named here and left alone
by both rounds, correctly — neither could make the change on its own branch
without guessing at the other's final shape.

The general form is worth keeping, because this programme will meet it again:
**a test can be made vacuous by a fix to code it does not test.** The
sweep-discipline family so far is about instruments that fail to land or measure
the wrong thing on their own. This is an instrument that was measuring correctly
against a defect, and that a *repair somewhere else* silently disarms. Nothing
in the test changes, nothing in the test's file changes, and the diff that does
it is in another module on another branch.

### And two things F-24's verifier found that belong to nobody

Both outside F-24's three limbs, both left untouched, neither numbered.

**Production source imports a test class.**
`src/Modules/Providers/Infrastructure/ProvidersServiceProvider.php:20` carries
`use Tests\Architecture\EveryRealDriverHasAnIdentityTesterTest;`. It predates
F-24, tracing to `515a425`. `LayeringTest` has nine rules and none of them looks
for a `Tests\` import in `src/` — the domain rule catches `\Http\` and
`\Infrastructure\Providers\`, the value-object rule catches
`Illuminate\Database`, and nothing catches the test namespace. A one-line rule
would close it, and the reason it matters is not tidiness: the autoloader in
production has no `Tests\` namespace, so this is a fatal error waiting on a code
path nobody has taken.

**`FakePaymentProvider::createPaymentIntent()` cannot fail.** Of everything
unrepresentable across the eight simulators, this is the one with money on it: a
decline is a *returned status*, not an exception, so "the customer was charged
and the answer was lost" cannot be written down. `REAL_PAYMENT_VERIFIED` is
`NONE` and no real PSP has ever been called, so nothing here is evidence about
production — but the shape that a platform most needs rehearsed is the one its
payment simulator cannot produce.

## Corrections owed from F-24, and why they wait for integration

F-24 is CLOSED and its branch is red by design, so integration must touch it
regardless. These two are shipped-code docblocks, recorded with exact text so
they cannot evaporate:

**The `[redacted]` arm's docblock claims reach it does not have.** It says *"This
is where it does"* of `RedactedJsonCast`'s promise, and the commit says the round
*"implements an invariant `RedactedJsonCast`'s docblock already promises"*. That
promise reads *"the handler receives `[redacted]`, which fails loudly, instead of
the platform quietly keeping a customer's root password in a table"* — and its
subject is **the handler, in production**. The fake fails loudly only in
simulation; against a real WHM or DirectAdmin adapter the promise is exactly as
unimplemented as before. The correction is one sentence: this is where the
invariant becomes *observable*, with F-45 still owning the production guard.

**`FakeDedicatedProvider`'s explanation names the wrong obstacle.** The decision
to leave the shape unwritten is right; the reason given — that no platform-level
consequence could be traced — is not. `AuthorisePxeBoot:137` calls
`setOneTimePxeBoot` and its catch at 138–157 already distinguishes the
indeterminate case deliberately and correctly, leaving the authorisation
standing because *"the controller may well have armed the override"*. The
consequence is traced and already handled. The real obstacle is that consuming
the arm requires a reset on the same marked address, and `setPower()` is gated by
the same address-keyed `assertReachable()`, so the reset throws first. Correct
the sentence, so the next round does not go looking for a consequence that is
already there and already right.

Both wait for integration rather than a round of their own. The rule this
programme wrote for deferrals — *an item deferred to a successor that does not
exist is an item lost* — is satisfied here and was not satisfied for F-37:
integration **must** touch this branch to land it at all, so the successor is
real and dated.

## I corrected two citations that were already right, and made them wrong

F-14's round fifteen was told, in its brief, that two line ranges *"no longer
locate their sentences"* and now sit at 2316–2325 and 2426–2435. It could not
confirm that, recorded the discrepancy in its commit message, and declined to
act on it. It was right to and I have verified it.

At `88d441c`, in `tests/Unit/SharedHosting/DirectAdminHostingProviderTest.php`:

```
2313  foreach (['/', '-', '.'] as $separator) {
2314      // Every width but four, which is the only one this rule may
2413      /*
2414       * THE ROW THAT PINS THE ORDER OF THE RULE'S TWO REMOVALS, and
```

Both **original** ranges contain their sentences. `:2313-2316` holds the "Every
width but four" comment; `:2413-2420` opens the docblock about the order of the
rule's two removals — its `/*` is the first line of the range.

And my replacements are worse than what they replaced. Line **2316** is a bare
`foreach ([1, 2, 3, ...] as $width) {`. Line **2426** is
`* And in FRONT of the date, which the prefix rule lets through` — the middle of
a sentence, not its start. So the correction did not merely fail to improve two
citations; it pointed both of them away from the thing they cited.

I also gave the file's path as `tests/Feature/SharedHosting/` in that brief. It
is `tests/Unit/SharedHosting/`.

### Why this one is worse than the transcription slips

The other figure errors in this programme have been *stale* — a count that was
true and drifted, a line number that moved under an edit. This is not that. The
citations were **correct at the sha I was writing about**, and I published a
correction to them anyway. Whatever I measured the drift against, it was not
`88d441c`, and I did not say which sha I had used because I did not notice I had
used a different one.

That is the same defect as the finding the round was working on. F-14's whole
subject is a measurement taken over one corpus and published as a claim about
another. My correction was a line-number measurement taken over one tree and
published as a claim about a different one. I spent the brief telling an agent
to re-derive every figure rather than carry mine, and the figure it should most
have distrusted was the one I had added on my own authority.

**The rule I am taking from it**: a correction to a citation is a measurement
like any other, and it must name the sha it was taken at. The ledger-row gate
enforces exactly this for status cells — a token in a status cell must appear in
the narrative — and the reason it keeps catching me is that I keep treating
provenance as something that goes without saying. It does not go without saying.
Every citation I publish from here names its sha.

The round's handling of it is the part to keep. It did not silently follow the
correction, and it did not silently ignore it. It checked, found both ranges
coherent, wrote down that either the correction was about a different file or it
was wrong, and carried on with the work. That is the third time in this
programme an agent has protected the record from me by declining to act on an
instruction that did not survive contact with the tree.

## A gate that checked consistency could not ask whether anything had been said

With eight agents running and nothing dispatchable, I started the cross-branch
overlap work that has been owed since the fifth stoppage. It needs each closed
finding's **integrating tip** — the commit an integrator should merge. Seventeen
of the thirty-seven closed rows did not name one.

`validate-ledger-rows.py` had been green over those seventeen for days, and it
was right to be, because it was asking the wrong question. It checked that every
slug and sha quoted in a status cell also appears in that row's narrative:
*is what you said consistent?* It had no way to ask *did you say anything?* A
CLOSED row with no sha is perfectly self-consistent and tells an integrator
nothing.

So the gate now has two halves that fail in opposite directions, and writing the
second immediately exposed the first working:

- **Completeness** turned red on 17 rows, forcing me to name a commit for each.
- **Consistency** then turned red on 8 of those, because I had put shas in status
  cells whose narratives never mentioned them — the same habit it has now caught
  me on six times.

Neither half is redundant. One asks whether the row is complete; the other asks
whether it is coherent; and a row can be either without being the other.

### What the seventeen turned out to be, and the trap inside them

**Nine are pre-programme closures** — F-01, F-02, F-03, F-05, F-06, F-07, F-09,
F-10, F-16 — closed before the branch-per-finding regime and therefore already
on the integration branch, with no `remediation/f<NN>` branch in existence.
Their honest answer is not a sha but *nothing to merge*, and they must now say
so in those words. That is not an escape hatch: the phrase is only accepted when
no branch exists for the finding, so a row that has one cannot use it to dodge.

**Eight needed archaeology, and one of them nearly went in wrong.** My first
rule for finding a tip was mechanical — take the `remediation/f<NN>*` branch
that is not an ancestor of a sibling — and it is wrong, for a reason that is a
genuine integration hazard rather than a bug in my script:

> **A worktree slug names a worktree, not a finding's work.** Three branches in
> this pool are named after a finding and carry none of it.
> `remediation/f32c`, `f20b` and `f13c` are **coordinator checkpoints** whose
> tips are integration-branch commits about entirely other findings —
> `f27c`'s tip is an **F-13** commit. F-32's round three is on
> `remediation/f32`; F-27's round three is on `remediation/f27`, at `a7a017a`,
> not on `f27c` at `8307a92`.

Merging `remediation/f32c` would pull a pile of unrelated coordinator commits
and silently omit F-32's actual work, and it would look like a successful merge.
I caught it only because `8307a92`'s subject line said `F-13:` while I was
writing it into F-27's row. Had F-13 used the older prose subject style, as
F-19, F-28 and F-35 do, nothing would have said a word.

The rule that actually works is to read the commits: **a finding's integrating
tip is the head of the branch whose commits-ahead-of-the-integration-branch are
that finding's own work.** I applied it to all eight and recorded, per row, how
many commits are behind the tip and what shape their subjects take — because
four of the eight predate the `F-NN:` prefix convention and a grep for the
finding number returns nothing for them. F-19's tip is reached through *"A
service ends because nothing was built for it"*, not through anything naming
F-19.

### The part I want to keep

Both of these are the same defect one level apart. The gate could not ask
whether a row had said anything; my tip-finder could not ask whether a branch
had done anything. Each substituted a cheap structural property — *is it
consistent*, *is it a leaf* — for the expensive semantic one, and each was green
over a real omission for as long as nobody needed the answer.

The integration would have needed the answer. That is the only reason either was
found now rather than in the middle of merging.

**The eight still-open findings are not in this table** and will add to it. The
figures are re-derivable from the ledger itself: take each `CLOSED` row's
integrating tip, diff it against its merge-base with the integration branch, and
union the paths.

### What the contended files need, which is not the same answer for each

**Three groups need no merge judgement at all, and two of them must not get one.**

- **`docs/openapi.yaml` (F-04, F-12, F-26) is generated.** Merging it textually
  is the wrong operation whatever the conflict looks like; it is regenerated
  with `php artisan openapi:generate` after the sources merge, and
  `--check` is the gate that says the regeneration landed. Its source,
  `resources/openapi/operations.php`, is hand-written and is a real merge.
- **The two `errors.php` catalogues (five findings each) and the two locale
  JSONs (three each)** are key/value catalogues where the expected conflict is
  additive. The risk is not the merge, it is a **duplicate key** or two findings
  rewording one shared message, neither of which a clean merge would report.
  Check keys as a set afterwards, in both languages, and diff the message text
  for keys more than one finding touched.
- **`.env.example` (F-08, F-26, F-37)** is where this programme has already made
  an arithmetic error about line distance. Additive; verify against
  `.env.testing.example`, which CI copies.

**Three are load-bearing infrastructure and want a real read.**
`tests/Feature/Queue/WorkerHarness.php` (F-04, F-13, F-29, F-31) is the harness
the entire thirteen-worktree pool runs through, and a bad merge there produces
failures in every finding at once, attributed to none of them.
`ConsolePermitConcurrencyTest.php` is touched by **five**.
`tests/Architecture/LayeringTest.php` (F-19, F-40) holds the rules everything
else is measured against.

**And one is already understood.** `docs/runbooks/drift.md` (F-22, F-39) is the
conflict I performed rather than predicted, written up above: the two findings
fixed one defect in opposite directions, the resolution is F-22's side plus a
`--write` plus one deleted register row, and my standing warning about that row
was wrong.

### The count is the reassuring part and the pattern is not

Eight percent contention across twenty-eight branches developed in isolation is
a good outcome for §7, and it is the strongest evidence I have that the
worktree-per-finding discipline paid for its considerable cost.

But look at *which* files they are. The top six are a translation catalogue, a
test harness, a route file, an OpenAPI source and two locale bundles — **shared
registries, not shared logic.** Almost nothing in `src/` is contended: the
module boundaries held. What findings collide over is the handful of
repository-wide lists that every feature has to add a line to, and those are
exactly the files where a clean textual merge is least informative about whether
the result is correct.
